questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a subclass equals that ignores the superclass rule

options.text: true,false, because the two bodies test different criteria.
false,false, because a Gift is not equal to a plain Item.
options.misconception: believes the subclass rule overrides the superclass rule

options.text: true,true, because both objects share the same id.
options.misconception: believes matching ids override the different test types

options.text: It fails to compile, because Gift.equals skips super.
options.misconception: believes calling the superclass is a compile-time requirement

questions.explanation: Item.equals accepts anything that is an Item with a matching id, so it accepts the Gift, while Gift.equals rejects anything that is not a Gift and never consults the superclass, giving true,false. Delegating to super.equals is the fix and the tempting omission, because a subclass often only wants to add a field, but the two bodies must agree on one criterion or the relation stops being an equivalence.
questions.hint: Run both equals bodies against both objects.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: predict the effect of short-circuit evaluation on a null argument
questions.stem: An equals body begins if (o == null || getClass() != o.getClass()) return false; and a caller executes item.equals(null). What happens?

options.text: It returns false immediately, before any field is touched.
It throws NullPointerException on the o.getClass() call.
options.misconception: believes the right operand of || is always evaluated

options.text: It returns true, because null equals any reference.
options.misconception: believes a null argument is a matching comparison

options.text: It returns false only when the classes happen to differ.
options.misconception: believes the class test is what rejects a null argument

questions.explanation: The o == null test short-circuits ahead of the getClass comparison, so the call returns false and no dereference happens. Throwing is the tempting worry, and the concern is well founded because writing the conditions in the other order would indeed throw on null, but || evaluates its left operand first and a true left operand skips the right one entirely.
questions.hint: || evaluates left to right and can skip the right side.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: state the hashCode obligation that follows from overriding equals
questions.stem: A class overrides equals to compare a String field called name but inherits hashCode from Object. What goes wrong when these objects go into a HashSet?

options.text: Equal objects can hash differently, so the set keeps both copies.
It fails to compile, because hashCode must be overridden too.
options.misconception: believes the compiler enforces the pairing of the two methods

options.text: The set still finds them, because contains calls equals on every item.
options.misconception: believes a set compares against all of its members

options.text: Equal objects are collapsed, because the hash decides equality.
options.misconception: believes the hash code itself determines set membership

questions.explanation: The contract says equal objects must have equal hash codes, and the inherited identity hash violates that, so two Items with the same name land in different buckets and a set can hold both. Duplicates being collapsed is the tempting reversal, and it matches the intuition that hashing decides membership, but the hash only selects a bucket while the equals call inside that bucket decides the match.
questions.hint: The hash picks the bucket; equals decides the match.
